chunks: As for what Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Wuhayb ibn Hafs from Abu Basir —
He said: I asked him about a snake that entered a large clay water jar (hubb) containing water and then exited from it. He said: If he finds other water, let him pour it out.

The correct interpretation of this is that it should be understood as a type of dislikedness (karahah), given the availability of water whose purity is certain. For this reason he commanded him to pour it out only if he finds other water. If it were ritually impure (najis), it would be obligatory to pour it out under all circumstances.

key_terms.إِرَاقَتِهِ: iraqa — the act of pouring out/discarding water; the operative legal consequence under discussion
key_terms.الْكَرَاهِيَةِ: ritual dislikedness (karahah/makruh) — a juristic category denoting an act that is discouraged but does not trigger impurity or prohibition
key_terms.حُبًّا: hubb — a large clay storage jar for water
key_terms.نَجِسًا: najis — ritually impure; a legal status that would impose an unconditional obligation to discard

ai.seo_question: Does a snake entering a water container render the water ritually impure (najis) according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Abu Basir asks an Imam about the ruling on water in a large clay jar (hubb) after a snake entered and exited. The Imam conditionally orders discarding the water only if other water is available. Shaykh al-Tusi (the compiler) interprets this conditional ruling as evidence of mere dislikedness (karahah), not ritual impurity (najasah), arguing that if the water were truly najis, disposing of it would be unconditionally obligatory regardless of whether alternative water is found.
